title: Formative vs summative assessment
description: Formative assessment checks learning in progress to guide next steps; summative assessment judges achievement at the end. How they differ and how to use both.
shortAnswer: Formative assessment gathers evidence of learning while it is happening and uses it to adjust teaching and give feedback, so the learner improves. Summative assessment judges what a learner has achieved at the end of a unit or program, usually for a grade, a pass, or a competency decision. The difference is purpose, not format: the same quiz can be formative or summative depending on how its results are used.
keyTakeaways: Formative assessment is assessment for learning; summative assessment is assessment of learning.
Black and Wiliam's 1998 review found firm evidence that strengthening formative feedback produces substantial learning gains.
In workplace and compliance training, summative results are what records and audits rely on.
Programs work best with formative checks throughout and a summative judgement at the end.

sections.heading: What is the core difference between formative and summative assessment?

blocks.text: The core difference is how the evidence is used: formative assessment feeds back into teaching and learning while there is still time to improve, and summative assessment records a judgement of achievement. Format does not decide the category; use does.

In their influential 1998 review, Paul Black and Dylan Wiliam defined formative assessment as "all those activities undertaken by teachers, and/or by their students, which provide information to be used as feedback to modify the teaching and learning activities in which they are engaged" ([Black and Wiliam, 1998](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/abs/10.1080/0969595980050102)).

They later refined this: practice is formative "to the extent that evidence about student achievement is elicited, interpreted, and used by teachers, learners, or their peers, to make decisions about the next steps in instruction" that are likely to be better than without that evidence ([Black and Wiliam, 2009](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11092-008-9068-5)). Summative assessment, by contrast, sums up achievement at a point in time, for certification, grading, or a [competency assessment](/glossary/competency-assessment) decision.

sections.heading: What does the research say about formative assessment?

blocks.text: The research says formative assessment, done well, reliably improves learning. Black and Wiliam's review reported that "Several studies show firm evidence that innovations designed to strengthen the frequent feedback that students receive about their learning yield substantial learning gains" ([Black and Wiliam, 1998](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/abs/10.1080/0969595980050102)).

The Australian Education Research Organisation (AERO), for example, states that formative assessment "has a strong evidence base that meets our highest standards of evidence", based on its review of 138 studies ([AERO](https://www.edresearch.edu.au/summaries-explainers/explainers/formative-assessment)). AERO also notes that regular formative assessment strengthens memory through the testing effect, and that students are likely to perform better in later summative tests.

Most of this evidence comes from schools and colleges. The mechanisms, feedback and retrieval practice, are general, but workplace programs should treat the size of effects as indicative rather than guaranteed. See [spaced repetition](/glossary/spaced-repetition) for a related technique.

Use formative assessment whenever people are still learning and can act on feedback; use summative assessment when a decision must be made and recorded, such as sign off to perform a task. In regulated training, summative assessment is usually mandatory and formative assessment is what makes it more likely people pass for the right reasons.

Summative judgements in regulated training can carry formal evidence rules. In Australia, for example, summative judgements in vocational training must follow the rules of evidence (validity, sufficiency, authenticity, and currency) set out by the Australian Skills Quality Authority (ASQA) under Standard 1.4 of the 2025 Standards for RTOs ([ASQA](https://www.asqa.gov.au/for-providers/standards-for-RTOs/practice-guides/quality-area-1-training-and-assessment/assessment-practice-guide)). Formative tasks do not carry that burden, which is exactly why they can be frequent and low stakes.

sections.heading: How do formative and summative assessment work together?

blocks.text: They work together when both are aligned to the same learning outcomes: formative checks rehearse and diagnose the outcomes that the summative assessment will judge. An [assessment blueprint](/glossary/assessment-blueprint) is the usual tool for planning this alignment.

sections.heading: How does Knowledge Foundry approach this?

blocks.text: Knowledge Foundry defines assessment points against the knowledge framework before content is written, and each point can be designated formative or summative. That keeps practice checks and final assessments aligned to the same concepts and outcomes, and makes clear which results belong in the training record.

faqs.q: Can the same test be both formative and summative?
faqs.a: Yes. What makes an assessment formative is that its results are used to guide next steps in learning. A test used to grade can also be formative if learners and trainers use the results to improve. Keeping the purposes explicit avoids confusing a practice attempt with a formal result.

faqs.q: Should formative assessment results be recorded?
faqs.a: They can be useful for spotting common misconceptions and improving content, but they are rarely part of the formal training record. Recording them as pass or fail can discourage honest attempts, which undermines their purpose.

faqs.q: Is a knowledge check in e-learning formative or summative?
faqs.a: Usually formative if it gives feedback and does not affect the outcome, and summative if it is scored against a pass mark that determines completion. Many modules use both: ungraded checks during the module and a graded assessment at the end.

Diagnostic assessment happens before learning to find out what people already know. It is closely related to formative assessment and can support recognition of prior learning or let experienced staff skip content they have already mastered.
